# The Ghost Fan: Diagnosing Persistent Heat in a 2006 Jeep Commander

When a 2006 Jeep Commander refuses to stop blowing hot air after you switch the climate control off, it feels like the system has entered an infinite loop. You aren't seeing code execution; you are seeing a mechanical state that hasn't reset. The symptoms describe a specific failure mode: the fan motor is receiving power or spinning on its own inertia, and the blend door actuator isn't engaging to block the hot air from the heater core.

This behavior usually points to a failure in the electrical switching logic rather than a simple resistor issue. In most automotive HVAC systems, turning off the fan switch doesn't physically cut power to the motor; it sends a signal to a relay or directly controls a low-voltage circuit that tells the motor to stop. If heat persists when the switch is off, but cooling works immediately after you toggle the switch back on and engage the A/C compressor clutch, the system has likely latched into a "stuck open" state for the blend doors or a shorted control circuit.

Think of the HVAC control module as a state machine. When you set the temperature to "off," the controller should transition the blend door motor to the closed position and cut power to the fan relay. If the air remains hot, the blend door is likely stuck in the "max heat" position. This is often caused by an actuator failure, where the electric motor holding the door in place has burned out or lost its return spring tension. However, the fact that you can restore cooling by toggling the fan switch and engaging A/C suggests the control logic is responsive enough to move the doors back to a default position upon receiving a new command sequence.

The most common root cause for this specific symptomâthe fan appearing to run on "low" when switched offâis a faulty resistor pack or a blown fan relay that is bypassing its resistance states. In older Chrysler vehicles like the Commander, the fan speed controller often consists of multiple resistors in series. When one fails short, the system defaults to full speed or a high-speed bypass. But since you can get cold air by engaging the A/C, the issue is more likely the blend door actuator.

To resolve this without replacing the entire HVAC box, start by isolating the blend door motor. The goal is to force the door back to its neutral position. Since the system responds to a command change (turning the fan back on), you can attempt to manually reset the actuator. Locate the actuator attached to the heater box, usually accessible from under the dashboard or through the glove compartment area. Disconnect the electrical connector and gently move the door linkage by hand to ensure it isn't physically jammed against a plastic stopper. Reconnect the plug and cycle the climate control settings: turn the fan off, wait 10 seconds, then turn it on high for 30 seconds before turning it back off. This power cycle can sometimes clear a software latch in the actuator controller that keeps the door open.

If manual cycling doesn't hold the position, the actuator itself is likely mechanically seized or electrically dead. Replacing the blend door actuator is a targeted fix that avoids the complexity of rebuilding the entire HVAC assembly. The trade-off here is time versus cost; replacing the actuator requires disassembling parts of the dash but saves the expense of a new climate control unit.

Before diving into mechanical repairs, verify the fan relay. If the relay contacts are pitted or stuck closed, it will feed continuous power to the fan motor regardless of the switch position. Locate the HVAC fuse box in the engine bay and inspect the relay for signs of melting or arcing. Swapping the relay with an identical one from a different circuit can confirm if the issue is electrical rather than mechanical. Once you identify whether the fault lies in the actuator's inability to close the door or the relay's inability to cut power, you can proceed with the specific repair that restores the intended thermal state without unnecessary part replacement.
